rationale: B wins by a slight margin because it is more ruthless about what has to be proven before anyone pitches. Its proof ask for "how 'no-show' was defined and whether late cancels were counted" is the kind of unglamorous detail that saves a founder from getting folded in the first reporter reply. A is strong, but "most boutique studios will never buy an AI tool" sneaks in an unsupported market claim and then asks the user to backfill it.
gaps_in_A: "The software behind 50,000 studios" quietly turns "50,000 studios and salons" into a cleaner but less accurate headline.
"most boutique studios will never buy an AI tool" is not in the update. Plausible is not the same thing as sourced.
"a private owner doesn't have to show public markets an AI revenue line" is a sharp thought, but it leans on a causal link the update does not provide.
"The prevailing pattern that reporter is tracking is AI as a paid add-on or premium tier" needs competitor evidence before it can carry a contrarian angle.
gaps_in_B: "The launch is live now" assumes public status too confidently, even though the set later catches itself with the embargo question.
"a boutique-fitness or salon trade outlet" overreaches the product audience. The assistant is for boutique fitness and wellness studios; salons are only in the platform footprint fact.
"Three shapes exist" undercounts the material. The update also supports a separate vertical-SaaS distribution angle around bundling AI into an incumbent booking platform.
